name: Walther's Law
statement: Facies that occur in conformable vertical succession must have formed in laterally adjacent depositional environments.
meaning: In an unbroken (conformable) stratigraphic sequence, the rock layers stacked on top of each other represent environments that once sat side by side across a landscape. As shorelines or other boundaries migrate through time, the vertical rock record comes to mirror the lateral arrangement of environments at any one moment. The law lets geologists read a single vertical core as a proxy for a horizontal map of past environments.
mechanism: When sea level rises (transgression) or falls (regression), the boundary between adjacent environments (beach, lagoon, offshore mud) migrates landward or seaward. A fixed vertical location therefore receives sediment from a succession of environments as their boundaries sweep past, so the vertical facies sequence duplicates the lateral sequence existing side by side at any time, but only where the succession is unbroken by an unconformity.

examples.text: A rising sea produces beach sand overlain by lagoonal mud overlain by offshore shale, matching the beach–lagoon–offshore belts that lay side by side along the original shoreline.
A prograding delta produces the reverse pattern, offshore mud overlain by delta-front sand overlain by delta-plain deposits, as the shoreline advances seaward.
In Russian-language geology the same principle is often called the Golovkinsky–Walther law, crediting Nikolai Golovkinsky’s independent earlier formulation.

whyItMatters: Walther’s law underpins sequence stratigraphy and facies-model interpretation, letting geologists reconstruct palaeogeography from a single borehole without lateral exposure. It is foundational to petroleum and coal exploration, where subsurface facies must be predicted between widely spaced wells.
limits: The law applies strictly only to conformable successions; any unconformity breaks the lateral–vertical correspondence. It also assumes gradual, continuous environmental migration rather than abrupt tectonic or climatic jumps, and it describes facies that must have been genuinely laterally adjacent.
misreadings: A common misreading applies the law across erosional surfaces or hiatuses, wrongly inferring lateral adjacency where the vertical contact is actually a gap in the record; the law is a rule about conformable sequences only.
origin: Formulated by German geologist Johannes Walther in 1894 in his work on the origin of sedimentary rocks; introduced to English-language literature via a 1973 translation by Gerard Middleton.

sources.text: "Johannes Walther’s Law of the Correlation of Facies," GSA Bulletin. — Walther’s 1894 original statement and Middleton’s 1973 translation.
Facies, Wikipedia. — the statement, the mechanism, and the Golovkinsky–Walther naming.
